title: Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 84, article 9 (2025); arXiv:2401.02843 (v3, 2025-10-08, read here)

cost.compute_notes: arXiv v3 PDF (38 pp) read via PyMuPDF; survey instrument PDF (75 pp) searched for exact wordings. OSF vmdny: 3 files, 12.4 MB, 3/3 hash-verified (cleaned anonymised response CSV, 3,270 rows x 461 cols; survey PDF; flow chart). NO analysis code deposited (paper: 'R 4.3.1, SPSS 29, Google Sheets'), so the aggregation was rebuilt from the text: per-respondent least-squares CDF fit to three year-probability pairs, mean of CDFs. About 5,000 fits per family; the whole run_all.sh takes a few minutes. A first Nelder-Mead implementation (12 starts) and the final trust-region one agree to the year on every HLMI quantile.

triggers: when do AI researchers expect human-level AI
probability AI causes human extinction according to AI researchers
expert survey on progress in AI ESPAI
aggregating expert forecast distributions by averaging CDFs

claims.statement: Aggregate forecast of AI researchers: 10% chance of High-Level Machine Intelligence (unaided machines better and cheaper than humans at every task) by 2027 and 50% by 2047, thirteen years earlier than the 2022 survey.
claims.scope: 2,778 respondents (15% of 18,459 reachable authors at six venues, $50 incentive), October 2023; HLMI block n = 1,714; half randomised to fixed-probabilities (years at 10/50/90%), half to fixed-years (probabilities at 10/20/40 years). Aggregate = mean of per-respondent gamma CDFs, both framings with equal weight.

quantities.name: hlmi_50pct_year_pooled
quantities.baseline: both framings pooled, gamma family; identical under lognormal and Weibull (reanalysis/e4.py)

quantities.name: hlmi_50pct_year_pooled
quantities.baseline: fixed-PROBABILITIES arm only; model-free median of the stated 50% answer: 20 years (2043)

quantities.name: hlmi_50pct_year_pooled
quantities.baseline: fixed-YEARS arm only; model-free median P(HLMI within 40 years) = 50%

quantities.name: hlmi_fixed_years_share_below_50pct_at_longest_horizon
quantities.baseline: fixed-years respondents giving < 50% at 40 years: their 50% year is extrapolated by the fitted family, not stated

our_assessment.why: Rebuilt from the data without the authors' code: 2048 (10% at 2027-2028) against the printed 2047 / 2027, and robust to the distribution family. But 2047 is the midpoint of two randomised framings that disagree by sixteen years (2041 vs 2057); the paper reports the framing effect and says it does not know which is more accurate, then averages them with equal weight. So the headline is a property of a 1:1 allocation ratio as much as of the respondents. The comparison with 2022 (-13 years) is valid only because both surveys used the same 1:1 mix; the within-survey framing gap is larger than the between-survey shift. Status `measures-something-else` on the pooled number when it is cited as 'when AI researchers expect HLMI' without the framing.

claims.statement: Full Automation of Labor (all occupations automatable) is forecast at 50% by 2116, about 70 years after HLMI although the two describe nearly the same event; the authors call the gap a possible framing effect.
claims.scope: FAOL block n = 774 (paper); fixed-years horizons 10/20/50 years.

quantities.name: faol_50pct_year_fixed_years_arm
quantities.baseline: fixed-years arm; not identified by the answers (see next row)

quantities.name: faol_fixed_years_share_below_50pct_at_longest_horizon
quantities.baseline: fixed-years respondents giving < 50% at 50 years; median P(FAOL within 50 years) = 10%

quantities.name: hlmi_faol_gap_model_free
quantities.unit: years (median stated 50% year: FAOL 75 vs HLMI 20)
quantities.source: reanalysis/e3.py, fixed-probabilities arms only (891 HLMI + 413 FAOL respondents, different people)

our_assessment.why: The HLMI-FAOL gap is real and needs no model: in the arm where respondents state years directly, the median 50% year is 20 years for HLMI and 75 for FAOL. What is NOT in the answers is the fixed-years half of the FAOL headline: 74% of those respondents never reach 50% within the 50 years they were asked about (median 10%), so their 50% year is set entirely by the tail of whichever distribution is fitted -- 2143, 2165 or 2222 for Weibull, gamma or lognormal -- and the pooled 90% point runs to the year 200,000+. The paper's sentence 'our analysis was insensitive to the value of this upper bound' (about 'never' coded as 100,000,000 years) is true of the 50% point and silent about the family. Quote FAOL from the fixed-probabilities arm (2090) or as a range, never as 2116 alone.

claims.statement: Answers to the three extinction questions were 'mostly consistent', with medians of 5% or 10%: AI advances causing human extinction or severe disempowerment (mean 16.2%, median 5%, n = 1,321); human inability to control future advanced AI causing it (19.4%, 10%, n = 661); the first within 100 years (14.4%, 5%, n = 655).
claims.scope: Each respondent saw at most one of the three (checked in the data). Wording verified in the deposited survey instrument.

quantities.name: ai_extinction_probability_median
quantities.baseline: Q1: 'future AI advances causing human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment'

quantities.name: ai_extinction_probability_median
quantities.baseline: Q2: 'human inability to control future advanced AI systems causing ...' -- a SUBSET of the Q1 event

quantities.name: ai_extinction_probability_median
quantities.baseline: Q3: Q1 restricted to the next 100 years -- also a subset

quantities.name: subset_superset_probability_of_superiority
quantities.unit: P(random Q2 answer > random Q1 answer), ties half

our_assessment.why: Every number reproduces. 'Mostly consistent' hides the one direction that matters: the control-problem question names a subset of the general question's event and receives the HIGHER probabilities (median 10 vs 5, p = 0.008), while the time-restricted subset is coherently lower. A between-subjects violation of extension, the signature of support-theory unpacking: naming a mechanism adds probability. The effect is small (probability of superiority 0.536) and must be quoted as small, but it means 'AI researchers put about 5% on extinction' and 'about 10%' are both instrument-relative: which one a reader hears depends on which wording they read.

artifacts.locator: https://osf.io/vmdny/ '2023 ESPAI - Cleaned and Anonymized Responses - espai2023 2024-01-08 redacted and clean data.csv'

checked.result: 3/3 files verified. 3,270 rows, of which 2,758 carry at least one cleaned answer and 512 carry none (paper: 2,778 responses; the file's 2,634 'Finished' rows are 94.8% of 2,778, matching the paper's '95%'). Checked 2026-10-16 after first writing an unverified sentence here. SPSS missing code '#NULL!'. Every extinction statistic in Table 2 reproduces exactly; HLMI/FAOL aggregates rebuild to within 1-5 years with n within 3% of the paper's. Insufficient in one respect: no analysis code, so the paper's exact fitting criterion and exclusion set cannot be confirmed -- the residual gaps (2048 vs 2047; 2111 vs 2116) are of that size.

datasheet.composition: One row per respondent; *_clean columns are the authors' cleaned answers; fixedprobabilities = framing arm (1/0).
datasheet.collection: Qualtrics, 5-24 October 2023, $50 or donation; 15% response rate.
datasheet.caveats: 'never' answers coded 100,000,000 years. Decreasing probability sequences were removed by the authors. Fixed-years HLMI horizon is 40 years, FAOL 50 (the paper explains the 40 as an inherited mistake).

relations.why: Same object -- elicited probabilities and dates of transformative or catastrophic AI -- and the same finding from a different manipulation: the response format moves the number. Karger: percentage vs 1-in-X, up to 800,000x on extinction. Here: fixed-years vs fixed-probabilities (16 years on the HLMI median), HLMI vs FAOL wording (55 years model-free), and a subset event judged more likely than its superset.

open_questions: Within-person check of the HLMI-FAOL gap is impossible here (different respondents got the two blocks). Did the 2016 or 2022 ESPAI give any respondent both?
Does the extinction subset effect (Q2 > Q1) replicate in the 2022 ESPAI (n = 149 / 162)? The printed medians are also 5% vs 10% there.

ANSWERED 2026-10-16 (reanalysis/e5_bounds.py; out/e5_bounds_*.txt) by partial identification: each respondent's CDF is trusted only up to their information horizon (longest horizon asked, or their own 90% year) and bounded in [F(h), 1] beyond it. HLMI 50%: 2048, identified interval [2048, 2049] -- robust. HLMI 90%: extrapolated point 2200, identified only as [2073, never]; the answers support at most 0.731 pooled probability. FAOL 50%: point 2111 (paper 2116), identified interval [2073, 2202] -- 129 years wide; the fixed-years arm alone never reaches 50% (max identified 0.252). FAOL 90%: unidentified. ORIGINAL: A pooled CDF of extrapolated individual tails: what is the pooled 90% point when every fixed-years fit is truncated at the longest asked horizon (treated as censored)? That is the honest upper quantile.
